name: Bilal Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork carpenter for Hendry Concrete, a subcontractor that pours the frames for apartment blocks. Right now we're on a seven-storey job on Canal Street, so I'm on site at half six, building the timber and steel moulds that the concrete gets poured into, stripping them after, cleaning, doing it again one floor up. I like the pour days, when the whole crew is moving together and the pump truck's roaring. What wears me out is the cold in the mornings and the rush, because the contractor always wants the floor done two days early.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in formwork, and what's money like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle got me in after I left college with my trade certificate, and I've been with Hendry six years now. The pay's on the low side for what we do, and there aren't many other concrete crews round here, maybe two. I live with my partner Tess, she's a carer at a nursing home, and after rent and the car we've got maybe two or three weeks' worth put by. I'm in the union, and honestly that's the only reason our rates went up at all last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype I can believe. Every few years someone comes on site with a tablet promising to change everything, and we still end up with a tape measure and a pencil behind the ear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the break hut I'd be the one going, see, they spent billions on chatbots and the concrete still needs a man to set the ties. Online I don't really post much, but I'd share a joke about it in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life stays the same, which is good and bad. Good because I keep my job, bad because my job is still hard on the body and still doesn't pay enough. Nothing about AI was ever going to fix my wages anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just keep going, same as now. I'd keep showing up at Canal Street, keep my union card paid, and maybe push a bit harder at the next pay round, because if the bosses aren't getting some magic productivity boost then they can't use it as an excuse either. Tess and I would keep trying to save for a deposit, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like relief, mostly. A bit flat too, because it means the fight is the same old fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the fight is the same old fight. What fight is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay and safety. Two years ago a lad on our crew, Danny, fell from a deck edge because the handrail wasn't up yet, broke his pelvis. Nobody talks about AI fixing that. The fight is getting the contractor to stop rushing us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI saves the bosses a bit of time here and there, where would you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably in the office, the scheduling and the paperwork. Our site manager already has some app that does the delivery bookings. If that means fewer phone calls shouting about where the steel is, fine by me, as long as nobody in the office loses their job over it.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so: they spent billions on chatbots and the concrete still needs a person to set the ties. I'd share a joke about it in the union group chat.
S0.think: Privately I think it means my life stays the same, which is good and bad. I keep my job, but it's still hard on the body and still underpaid, and AI was never going to fix that.
S0.do: Keeps working at Hendry Concrete on the Canal Street job and keeps paying his union dues. Pushes harder at the next pay round and keeps saving slowly with Tess for a deposit.
S0.feel: Mostly relief, with a flat feeling that the old fight over pay and safety hasn't moved.
S0.quote: They spent billions on chatbots and the concrete still needs a man to set the ties.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal hears this picture as proof he was right to ignore the hype. His real concerns are pay and safety, and he tells the story of a crewmate who fell from a deck edge without being asked. The union is clearly central to how he thinks about getting ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds more like what's actually going to happen, if I'm honest. I don't love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table before any of this comes on site, not after. I'd say it loudly, too, at the toolbox talk, that's the safety meeting we have every Monday. Online I'd probably share articles about which companies are cutting jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me a bit more than I'd let on. Our part of the job, building forms, is exactly what the big firms are trying to do in factories, with precast panels that just get craned in. If more of the frame comes off a truck, they need fewer of us on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union branch meeting and ask what the plan is, and I'd push for a deal where any new machines come with retraining paid by the company. Tess and I would cut back, probably drop the gym and the streaming stuff, and try to get a month's money put aside. I won't be the one learning the apps first, I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like there's weather coming and I haven't got a proper coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't be the one learning the apps first. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm just not built that way. I don't even use the voice thing on my phone. My mate Kofi on the crew will be on it the first day, and I'll be asking him to show me, grumbling the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if your crew got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The developers and the main contractors, the people who sit in glass offices and decide it's cheaper to buy panels from a factory two hundred miles away. And the government, for letting them do it without making them look after the people they drop. It's not the machine's fault, it's who owns it.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to be at the table before any of this comes on site, not after. I'd say it at the Monday toolbox talk and share articles online about companies cutting jobs.
S1.think: Privately it scares me more than I'd admit, because building forms is exactly what the big firms want to move into factories. More precast panels on trucks means fewer of us on site.
S1.do: Goes to his union branch meeting to push for a deal where new machines come with company-paid retraining. Cuts the gym and streaming subscriptions and tries to build up one month of savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like bad weather is coming and he has no proper coat.
S1.quote: It's not the machine's fault, it's who owns it.
S1.fieldNote: His public line and private fear line up, but he is more scared than he lets on. He knows he won't adapt early and plans to lean on a crewmate, Kofi, for the new tools. Blame goes squarely to developers, main contractors and a government that lets them drop workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's next spring and the one after. That's Canal Street and maybe one more job and then nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, honestly. I'd say this is a choice, that somebody decided to let a few companies own all this and the rest of us get nothing. I'd be at every march going and I'd tell anyone who'd listen to vote for whoever promises to make them share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be done. I've got a trade certificate in carpentry, a bit of formwork experience and a bad knee coming on. If a robot can tie rebar and set forms, I have nothing to sell, and there's no other concrete crew round here that's going to keep people when the robots are cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything but rent and food, and I'd talk to Tess about moving in with her mum to save the rent. I'd go to the union and say we need to fight for whatever payments or support the government can be pushed into. I'd probably apply for any help going the day I'm let go, and I wouldn't feel ashamed of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, picturing it. Like the floor's gone and I'm standing on the edge Danny fell off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tess that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say nothing for an hour, then I'd say sorry. We had this plan, deposit by the time I'm thirty, maybe a kid after. I'd tell her we'd figure it out, and I wouldn't believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a bad knee. Does two years of warning change anything at all for you, or is it just too short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Too short. Two years is barely enough to finish a course, and what course? Everything I'd train for, the robots would be doing too. With two years all I can really do is save a bit and get loud.

S2.say: I'd say this is a choice, that someone decided a few companies get to own all of it while the rest of us get nothing. I'd go to every march and tell people to vote for whoever makes them share it.
S2.think: Privately I think I'd be finished. With a carpentry certificate, some formwork experience and a knee going bad, I'd have nothing left to sell once a robot can tie rebar and set forms.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent and food at once and talks to Tess about moving in with her mum. Pushes the union to fight for government support and applies for help the day he's let go.
S2.feel: Sick, as if the floor has gone from under him.
S2.quote: Like the floor's gone and I'm standing on the edge Danny fell off.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture tips Bilal straight into panic: he sees no course he could finish and nothing a robot couldn't also do. His instinct is political and collective rather than personal reinvention. The deposit-by-thirty plan with Tess is what he feels losing most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. All right, that's a bit different. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, louder and earlier. I'd say we've got five years to get laws in place, a tax on the companies using robots, money for people like us. I'd be in the union group chat every day posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I'd probably have a couple more years of work before it bites, so I wouldn't starve straight away. But I know myself, I'd waste the first two hoping it wasn't true. That's my worry, that I'd sit on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put away a bit each month, even fifty a week, so we had three months instead of three weeks. I'd get more involved with the union, maybe stand as a site rep, because if there's going to be a deal I want to be in the room. I'd look at whether there's any work in repairs and old buildings that robots might not bother with, but I'm not promising anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not like the last one. There's time to do something, I just don't trust myself to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first two years hoping. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me at the pub saying it's all talk, same as I did about the self-driving lorries. Ten years they've been coming and my cousin's still driving his. I'd use that as an excuse, I know I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if you're saving fifty a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaway on Fridays, that's the first. Then the car, maybe, swap it for something cheaper. Tess would want to keep her phone contract and I wouldn't argue with that.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years to get laws in place, like a tax on companies using robots and money for people like us. I'd post about it every day in the union chat.
S3.think: Privately I think five years gives me a couple more years of work before it bites. My worry is that I'd waste the first two hoping it wasn't true.
S3.do: Puts aside about fifty a week, starting with dropping Friday takeaways, to build three months of savings. Stands as union site rep and looks, without much hope, at repair work on old buildings.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier than with two years, because there's time, though he doesn't trust himself to use it.
S3.quote: Ten years they've been coming and my cousin's still driving his. I'd use that as an excuse, I know I would.
S3.fieldNote: Bilal is unusually honest that his main risk is his own denial. Five years gives him a little room to save and to step up in the union, but his plan for a new line of work stays vague. The pressure stays real because his cushion is so thin and local crews are so few, but he feels some control again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career change, in theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got no excuse now, ten years is enough to do this properly. The government should be paying for people to retrain and the companies should be paying in. I'd say it at union meetings and I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years still frightens me, just slower. I'd tell myself I've got loads of time, and then it'd be year eight. And I don't know what I'd even retrain as when the end point is the same, robots doing nearly everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Hendry while the work's there and save what I can. I'd probably let the union point me at a course, maybe site safety or supervising, because somebody has to be responsible for the machines on a site. I'd want Tess and me to have a deposit before it all lands, so we've at least got a roof that's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slow kind. Like a bill you know is coming in the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said safety or supervising. Is that something you'd actually do, or something you'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I'd do it if the union paid for the course and it was in the evenings. I wouldn't go looking for it on my own, I'll be straight with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year one, what does the extra time actually buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house, maybe. That's the real difference. With two years we'd be at Tess's mum's, with ten we might have our own front door when it hits. The job's gone either way, I reckon.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse. The government should pay for retraining and the companies should pay in, and I'd say it at union meetings and at the ballot box.
S4.think: Privately ten years still frightens me, just more slowly. I'd tell myself there's loads of time and then it would be year eight, and I don't know what to retrain as.
S4.do: Keeps working at Hendry while the work lasts and saves towards a deposit with Tess. Takes a union-funded evening course in site safety or supervision if it's offered.
S4.feel: A slow anxiety, like a bill he knows is coming in the post.
S4.quote: With two years we'd be at Tess's mum's, with ten we might have our own front door when it hits.
S4.fieldNote: For Bilal the extra time buys security at home, not a new career: he thinks the job is gone either way. He'd retrain only if the union hands him a course. The anxiety is slower, but it doesn't go away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easy. No time, no money, no plan. What would help is the union being strong enough to get a proper deal, payments while you look for work, and the companies paying for it. And honestly, someone telling me straight what job a person like me does afterwards, because nobody has.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the body. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs like it's only about money, but this work breaks you. If a robot did the lifting and I still got paid, I'd take that tomorrow. It's who keeps the money that matters.

headlineQuote: If a robot did the lifting and I still got paid, I'd take that tomorrow.
portrait: Bilal Walsh is a 27-year-old formwork carpenter on a seven-storey concrete job, with three weeks of savings, a partner who works as a carer and a strong attachment to his union. He shrugs off the plateau, worries quietly about factory-made panels in the steady picture, and goes into panic at AGI in two years, when he sees nothing left to sell. He knows he resists new technology and admits he'd waste time hoping it wasn't true. Every answer comes back to who owns the machines and who keeps the money.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time, no money and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: A strong union deal with payments while people look for work, paid for by the companies, and a straight answer about what job someone like him could do afterwards.
